Where it began

Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi was born in Bhopal on 5 January 1941, and cricket was in the family. His father, Iftikhar Ali Khan Pataudi, was a celebrated cricketer himself, and the trophy England and India play for in Test series was later named after him.

Young Mansoor went to school in Aligarh and Dehradun before heading to England, to Lockers Park in Hertfordshire, where Frank Woolley coached him, and then to Winchester College. There he was a batting prodigy. As captain of the school side in 1959 he made 1,068 runs in a season, beating a record Douglas Jardine had set in 1919. He was 16 when he first played for Sussex, in 1957, and at Oxford, where he read Arabic and French at Balliol, he became the university's first Indian captain.

The player

His Test career began against England in Delhi in December 1961. In the last Test of that series, at Madras, he made 103 and helped India to their first series win over England. A few months later, in the West Indies, he was asked to lead the side at 21 years and 77 days, the youngest Test captain in the world until 2004.

He played 46 Tests from 1961 to 1975, making 2,793 runs at 34.91 with six hundreds, the best of them an unbeaten 203. He led India in 40 of them. The highlight came in New Zealand in 1968, when his team won India's first Test abroad and went on to take the series, the first they had ever won overseas.

What made him special

Everyone called him Tiger, and he fielded like one. John Arlott and Ted Dexter both rated him the finest fielder in the world in his day, and he held 27 Test catches. He also had patience to go with his flair, and in one Test at number six he faced 554 balls, a Test record for a number six.

Bowling was another matter. He sent down his medium pace from time to time and took one Test wicket, which he was perhaps wise not to try to improve upon.

Away from the middle

He played 137 first-class matches for Sussex and captained the county in 1966. In 1968 he married Sharmila Tagore, and the same year Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year. He wrote an autobiography, Tiger's Tale, in 1969. India gave him the Arjuna Award and the Padma Shri, and the BCCI gave him its highest award for a former player, the C. K. Nayudu award, in 2001. In later years he managed the Indian team, refereed two Ashes Tests in 1993 and sat on the council of the Indian Premier League. He died in 2011.

And finally

In 2013 the BCCI began a memorial lecture in his name, and Sunil Gavaskar gave the first one. It is a fitting tribute to a captain who always made people listen.
